title: Bayesian Downscaling of Satellite-Derived Solar-Induced Chlorophyll Fluorescence
summary: We present an extendable Bayesian framework for spatial downscaling of satellite-derived measurements with coarse, irregular footprints. Motivated by measurements of solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) from the earth-observing OCO-2 satellite, we model coarse-resolution observations as noisy, weighted averages over an underlying fine-resolution spatial field. The latent process is defined over a regular grid and regularized using a Simultaneous Autoregressive (SAR) prior, yielding a sparse precision structure that enforces spatial smoothness. This formulation enables efficient posterior inference including uncertainty quantification and naturally accommodates land cover information through modified neighborhood structures or covariates. To assess accuracy, we conduct a semi-synthetic validation using albedo data derived from Sentinel-2 satellite surface reflectance, finding strong correspondence between posterior means and the synthetic generating field (R2 = 0.72 when including the proportion of water as a covariate and 0.57 without any covariates). We apply our method to a high-density OCO-2 target mode SIF observations over Boston, demonstrating that it produces fine-resolution posterior maps that reflect heterogeneity in urban environments and align with greenness, with a moderate relationship with the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) (R2 = 0.417 for pixels with 20+ overlapping soundings, 0.323 overall). Our approach achieves high-resolution recovery of satellite measurements with principled uncertainty quantification.

title: Can We Trust Evaluations of AI Weather Forecasts for Extremes? How Evaluation Protocols Shape Model Rankings
comment: Accepted paper at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: TAE (Trust-AI-Eval): Can We Trust AI Evaluation?
summary: AI weather models perform competitively with traditional physics-based models at a fraction of the computational cost, and they are thus already used operationally. However, studies reach conflicting conclusions about their ability to forecast extreme weather events, and comparisons across studies are complicated by differing evaluation protocols. We discuss the challenges that arise when comparing AI and physics-based weather forecasts for extreme events. Within a common experimental design, we find that model rankings are highly sensitive to the choice of evaluation metrics: the considered physics-based model tends to perform best when evaluation is restricted to observed extreme events, whereas AI models generally perform better when evaluated using weighted scoring functions. A contingency table analysis shows that AI models underpredict the frequency of extremes, so that their scores are generally dominated by misses, while the physics-based model forecasts extremes more frequently and its scores are dominated by false alarms. Different evaluation metrics penalise these errors differently. Further score decompositions confirm that the score differences arise primarily from miscalibration rather than discrimination ability. This sheds light on the contrasting results in the literature, and highlights the importance of the evaluation metrics used to evaluate AI models.

title: A Physically-Motivated Stochastic Model of Tropical Cyclone Dynamic Wind Fields
summary: Tropical cyclones (TCs) pose significant risk to infrastructure and human safety, and the frequency and intensity of large TCs are expected to increase in the future. Quantifying such risk to coastal and inland regions is challenging, largely due to the rare nature of TCs which limits historical data availability. We introduce a new stochastic model of TC wind fields conditional on a small number of physical variables commonly found in synthetic and observed storm track databases. The model consists of a physically-motivated mean trend and an expansion of the residual field into a wavelet frame. We demonstrate the approach on a dataset consisting of historical data for storms impacting the northwest Gulf of Mexico. The model adequately captures asymmetry and nonstationary space-time correlation structures of observed wind fields.

title: Causal inference in staggered adoption panels: The correct comparison set depends on your intervention
summary: A powerful data structure for causal inference is staggered adoption: many units are observed over many time periods, during which some units adopt an irreversible treatment at various time points while others remain untreated. Popular methods that apply in this setting include difference in difference, fixed effects, matching, and synthetic control. All of these methods compare the future outcomes of treatment adopters and non-adopters to answer the question: for units who adopt treatment, what outcomes would have been realized if they had remained untreated? We show that this question actually hides two very different causal questions of interest. The first is what would have happened under a momentary intervention to prevent treatment at its factual adoption time. The second is what would have happened to a treated unit under a longitudinal ban preventing treatment at all periods until outcome measurement. We show how to answer each question under conditionally ignorable treatment adoption or under parallel trends. We highlight that common methods cannot answer the second question because this question requires a time-varying comparison set with time-varying weights.

title: Sequential Monte Carlo Sampling of Feasible Regions Represented by R-Functions
summary:
Feasible-region sampling and volume estimation become increasingly inefficient when constraints define only a small fraction of a convenient bounding domain. We combine R-functions, which encode compound feasibility as a continuous signed field, with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) samplers. The proposed construction exploits not only the sign of the R-function, which determines exact feasibility, but also its continuous negative values outside the feasible set, which provide graded information on constraint violation. Logistic intermediate distributions use this information to guide particles progressively towards feasibility, while the final target distribution remains uniform on the feasible region.
  Experiments on intersections and unions, including disconnected cases of hyperballs, show substantial variance reductions relative to direct rejection sampling, with the statistical advantage generally increasing as the feasible fraction decreases. For sufficiently small feasible regions, these advantages persist even after accounting for computational cost. To isolate the benefit of continuous R-function information, we also compare the proposed method with an SMC sampler with a region-only (RO) construction that uses the same sequential particle machinery but retains only binary feasible/infeasible information. We demonstrate that the R-function-informed SMC method concentrates particles in the feasible region earlier and produces lower-variance volume estimates than RO.

title: An F-Type Normal-Reference Calibration for High-Dimensional Covariance Testing
comment: 50 pages, 2 figures. Includes appendices and ancillary code
summary: An F-type normal-reference calibration is developed for testing equality of two high-dimensional covariance matrices with unknown means. The test statistic is a ratio whose numerator measures the Frobenius covariance discrepancy and whose denominator estimates its null expectation. Their difference is the complete Li-Chen statistic. Under suitable moment and trace conditions, we establish a Gaussian-reference approximation. After standardization, the statistic and its reference share the normal or nonnormal limits determined by a convergent normalized spectrum. The reference is a ratio of independent chi-square-type mixtures. Applying Welch-Satterthwaite matching to its two components gives an ordinary F approximation, with degrees of freedom estimated from independent four-observation blocks. The effect of estimating the population means is controlled by an exact expansion, and local-power and consistency results are established. The ordinary F approximation is asymptotically valid under a diffuse spectrum, whereas a covariance spike can produce a nonvanishing approximation error. Simulation studies examine empirical size and power under normal and nonnormal sampling. Averaging the trace estimates over fixed partitions improves their stability, but does not remove size inflation in the strongly correlated settings.

title: Bridge change-of-measure for propagator estimation of diffusions
summary: The propagator of one-dimensional diffusions has relevant applications in statistical inference and across many disciplines. Yet it is obtained in closed form only for very few simple models. Here we analyze an importance sampling strategy based on a bridge change of measure to estimate propagators: paths are generated under an auxiliary diffusion whose bridge between the two fixed boundary points is easy to generate, and the target propagator is recovered through a Radon-Nikodym derivative or likelihood ratio correction derived from Girsanov's theorem. This method overcomes the main limitations of the crude Monte Carlo estimator, which relies on binning in state space, introducing bias and becoming inefficient with rare transitions. We apply the method to a range of benchmark processes and show that the bridge-based estimator matches the accuracy of crude Monte Carlo with orders of magnitude fewer sample paths. Finally, we elaborate on discretization schemes for the Radon-Nikodym derivative and on approximations to the best-in-class change of measure, both of which increase the efficiency of the method.

title: Why Constrained Updates Still Forget: A Functional-Path Analysis of Continual SFT
summary: Supervised fine-tuning adapts language models to specialized tasks but can disrupt previously acquired behavior. Existing approaches constrain parameters, gradients, or replay objectives, yet the connection between the protected object, the intervening trajectory, and retained outputs remains unclear. We develop a functional-path account that decomposes old-loss changes along realized updates into the controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects. The account yields a conditional refresh budget and identifies the restoring direction supplied by informative replay. Matched QLoRA interventions separate constraint granularity from placement before or after Adam: placement strongly affects retention across the studied code-label audits, whereas the granularity interaction depends on the endpoint. Checkpointed generation separates endpoint recovery from higher sampled-path accuracy, and matched replay schedules reveal loss exposure concealed by final scores. A sequential-task comparison extends this distinction to backward transfer: subspace regularization and projection improve average retention while trading off different old tasks; supervised replay protects both more consistently in this setting. Additional response interfaces distinguish content gains from exact-response retention. These findings connect update-level protection to task-wise behavior and motivate mitigation through explicit functional anchors, trajectory evaluation, and joint old/new auditing.

title: A Bayesian Copula Dirichlet Process GLM for Longitudinal Data
summary: We introduce a semiparametric Bayesian generalized linear model (GLM) for longitudinal continuous outcomes that preserves the usual interpretation of the GLM regression structure while leaving the baseline distribution nonparametric. The proposed copula Dirichlet process generalized linear model (CDPGLM) combines a Dirichlet process prior for the baseline distribution, a parametric GLM regression structure for covariate effects, and a copula for longitudinal within--subject dependence. This construction separates modeling the marginal distribution of an individual repeated measurement from modeling the association: the Dirichlet process GLM component defines the marginal density and regression mean, whereas the copula captures dependence among repeated measurements. Compared with a parametric beta mixed--effects model, the CDPGLM provides similarly efficient estimation of regression effects while being substantially more robust to estimate marginal distributions and lower-tail probabilities (the complement of exceedance probability). In an application to data from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) Lung Health Study, the CDPGLM and a parametric mixed beta model gave comparable inference on regression coefficients, but the CDPGLM more closely matched the empirical marginal distribution and reported more realistic and detailed lower--tail risk summaries.

title: The Hammock Plot: Where Categorical and Numerical Data Relax Together
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the Stata Journal
summary: Effective methods for visualizing data involving multiple variables, including categorical ones, are limited. The hammock plot (Schonlau 2003) visualizes both categorical and numerical variables using parallel coordinates. We introduce the Stata implementation hammock. We give numerous examples that explore highlighting, missing values, putting axes on the same scale, and tracing an observation across variables. Further, we discuss parallel univariate plots as an edge case of hammock plots. We also present and make publicly available a new dataset on the 2020 Tour de France.

title: Sharp convergence rate of the estimation error of LASSO via the Feature Space Decomposition method
summary: In this paper, we use the Feature Space Decomposition (FSD) method to establish an explicit, non-asymptotic, instance-optimal convergence rate for the estimation error of the LASSO in the Gaussian linear regression problem for any signal, any diagonal covariance and any regularization parameter above $σ_ξ/\sqrt{N}$ where $σ_ξ$ is the noise variance and $N$ the number of data.

title: Tag loss models for capture-recapture data without double tagging
summary: Standard capture-recapture (CR) models assume that marked individuals do not lose their tags during the sampling period. When this assumption is violated, the estimates of model parameters can be biased. Existing tag-loss models generally rely on double-tagging all or a subset of captured individuals, permanent marks, or auxiliary information on tag retention. However, double-tagging and permanent marking may be impractical, and reliable auxiliary information may be unavailable or difficult to obtain in many situations. In this paper, we develop a novel latent multinomial modelling framework for analysis of CR data with tag loss, without requiring double-tagging or permanent marking. The proposed model framework applies to both closed-population and open-population Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS) settings. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that key model parameters can be reliably estimated in both settings. We illustrate the application of the method using a dataset from a long-term study on elephant seals. The results suggest that robust inference on tag loss and demographic parameters can be achieved without double tagging, thereby avoiding logistical challenges and broadening the framework's applicability to a wider range of studies.

title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via Generalized Moment Matching
summary: We study $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differentially private synthetic data for arbitrary databases of $n$ records in $[-1,1]^d$ under a specified integral probability metric (IPM). We introduce generalized moment matching, which estimates moments privately, fits a probability measure, and samples synthetic records. A general error theorem applies when moment error controls the target IPM. This framework extends Chebyshev moment matching for $1$-Wasserstein distance and smooth queries. We apply the framework to maximum mean discrepancy with Matern and Laplace kernels and a two-layer ReLU neural tangent kernel.We also obtain guarantees for sliced Wasserstein-$1$ and the IPM induced by norm-bounded ReLU networks. With sufficiently many synthetic records,these rates are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed dimension.

title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
summary: Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.

title: Snapshot plots: displaying summary tables as parallel univariate plots with consistent color highlighting
summary: For empirical studies, social and health scientists give background characteristics of their sample and summarize them in the famous "Table 1". When treatment/ control groups are present, this table gives summary statistics by group to see whether the background characteristics differ by group. We propose snapshot plots --- parallel univariate plots with consistent highlighting --- to visualize such tables. Compared to "Table 1", such plots are designed to facilitate comparisons of background characteristics --- in particular among groups --- and give more detail on numerical variables. We provide a web app as well as a python implementation of snapshot plots. Snapshot plots arise as edge cases of hammock plots (parallel coordinate plots for mixed categorical/ numerical data). We demonstrate the usefulness of snapshot plots for two "Table 1"s.

title: Finite-Query Coherent Projection of Black-Box Conditional Predictions
summary: Local conditional predictions from a black box need not admit a common joint distribution. We study two aspects of their coherent projection: finite-access precision and directional fidelity. For arbitrary deterministic binary conditional tables, we establish matching expected minimax excess conditional-Kullback--Leibler risk $Θ(\min\{R\sqrt{d/B},d^2/B\})$ under independent uniform exact-table queries, with repeated draws charged, for a local bounded pairwise joint class. The result holds for sufficiently large $d$, $R\sqrt d\le M_0$, and $Cd^3\le B\le(d2^{d-1})^{1/3}$, where $M_0$ is fixed. A moment estimator attains the upper bound. The main technical contribution is a matching lower-bound construction that respects shared pairwise interactions and frozen exact-table responses, with comparison to the best projection of the same realized table. We then examine directional fidelity in a computable hard-marginal formulation that preserves direct black-box marginals. A preregistered TabPFN-v2 case study combines a Car anchor with a frozen two-dataset, three-split extension. All $1{,}152$ extension optimization instances pass independent numerical checks at registered tolerances. Directional contrasts are dataset-dependent and asymmetric: optimizing one direction need not improve the other. Together, the analyses distinguish accurate approximation of a selected projection from improvement in conditional directions outside its fitted objective.

title: High-Value Training Data from Noisy, Diverse Sources
summary: Training state-of-the-art models increasingly requires learning from large, heterogeneous datasets whose examples vary in quality, domain relevance, and source of supervision. Dataweighting---assigning different weights to training examples---offers a general way to control how such data influences training, but learning effective weights at scale remains challenging. We develop a scalable approach to learning dataweights: given a small, high-quality target dataset, we use metagradients through the training process to efficiently optimize training-example weights directly for performance on the target domain. To scale beyond a fixed dataset and model, we learn parametric weighting rules that generalize to new and streaming examples and transfer from smaller models to substantially larger ones. We study reward modeling as a prototypical application, where preference data may be noisy, adversarial, synthetic, or mismatched with the target domain. Learned dataweights improve held-out performance, automatically adapt reward models to specialized domains, and allow mixtures of human and synthetic supervision to outperform either source alone.

title: Functional Inference for the Mean Curve of Intraday Spot Correlation
summary: In this paper, we propose estimators for the mean of the daily spot-correlation curves, which are robust to the presence of finite-variation jumps in the price processes. The related feasible functional central limit theorems for the proposed estimators have been established under a joint infill and long-span setting. Based on the asymptotic theory, we develop a test procedure for flatness of the curves. Monte Carlo simulations confirm the strong finite-sample performance of the estimators. In an empirical application to 30 U.S. stocks from 2010 to 2019, we find a pronounced end-of-day surge in the mean of correlation curves across diverse stock groupings, alongside substantial calendar-time non-flatness in the curves.

title: Rematching Estimators for Average Treatment Effects
summary: Matching estimators are widely applied in practice for their great intuitive appeal. However, simple matching estimators with a fixed number of matches ($M_0$) are generally inefficient. In this article, we propose matching estimators with a variable number of matches to gain efficiency via rematching. Rather than increasing $M_0$ to gain precision, which introduces an increase in bias, the key is to rematch the treated units from the opposite direction to utilize unmatched control units. Our rematching estimators are applicable to both the average treatment effect and its counterpart for the treated population. The proposed rematching estimators are proven asymptotically valid and uniformly more efficient than matching estimators with the same $M_0$. Simulation results confirm that the proposed rematching estimators substantially improve the simple matching estimators in finite samples. As an empirical illustration, we apply the estimators proposed in this article to the National Supported Work data.

title: Flow-based Spectral Kernel Learning for Nonstationary Attention
summary: Kernelized attention provides a useful perspective for understanding self-attention as a similarity-based aggregation mechanism, but existing approaches often rely on fixed or stationary kernels, limiting their ability to adapt the similarity structure to complex token interactions. In this paper, we propose flow-based spectral kernel attention (FSKA), a framework for learning expressive nonstationary attention kernels. FSKA formulates kernelized attention through spectral density learning and parameterizes the resulting bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows. This design enables flexible and regularizable kernel learning while remaining compatible with scalable linear-attention computation. We further show that expressive kernel learning enables a simplified attention design with removed query--key projections and fixed orthogonal value projections, resulting in a more parameter-efficient architecture. Controlled experiments on classification, ablation, and scalability profiling show that FSKA achieves competitive or improved performance over existing attention mechanisms, while reducing projection-related trainable parameters by approximately $40\%$--$47\%$ compared with most baselines and maintaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling. Code Available: https://github.com/ziyang18/FSKA.

title: Beyond Global Importance: A Heterogeneity Index for Sensitivity Analysis
summary: Global sensitivity analysis quantifies how strongly inputs influence a model output, however, input importance often varies across the model space. We introduce a heterogeneity index H to quantify this variation. The index compares normalized regional sensitivity profiles using mean pairwise total-variation distance and its values range from zero to one. We test H on nine benchmark functions and examine its robustness to the number of regions, sample size, and sampling strategy. We further demonstrate it using models of wooden-pallet carbon footprint, flood risk, and steel-structure reliability. Across these cases, H reveals changes in sensitivity that global indices obscure, including inputs whose importance changes substantially across the model space and differences between rare behavioral regimes. The index complements global sensitivity analysis by indicating when a single global sensitivity profile is insufficient. An open-source implementation is provided in the simdec package.

title: Is Spectral Self-Supervised Learning a Minimax Optimal Method of Density Ratio Estimation?
summary: Spectral self-supervised learning is a method of density ratio estimation for the setting in which only samples drawn from the joint density of the numerator are available. The method has extensively been studied in terms of the computational properties, such as optimal solutions and connections to representation learning. However, theoretical understanding of its statistical property is still insufficient. In this work, we study three questions, namely, the minimax optimality, the applicability of the theory to regularized algorithms, and the statistical merits of density ratio estimation with data augmentation mechanisms that have recently been considered in the context of self-supervised representation learning. We first show that for general classes of Hölder continuous density ratios, there are regularized spectral self-supervised learning algorithms that yield estimators attaining the minimax optimality, up to logarithmic factors. We then prove that for subclasses endowed with a data augmentation mechanism, we obtain faster convergence rates that are also minimax optimal (up to logarithmic factors) in a weaker sense. We also present the key proof ideas tailored for self-supervised density ratio estimation.

title: Lifetime-valid decisions by continually evolving AI analysts
summary: AI agents increasingly act as analysts whose decision can often be cast as hypothesis tests. Classical tests control the Type I error rate, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, for fixed procedures. However, AI analysts introduce internal randomness and can evolve continuously over time. As AI analysts evolve, the risk of approving versions with Type I error rates above the target can accumulate, and adaptive use of evaluation feedback can lead to overfitting. We introduce continual validation, which evaluates each proposed AI analyst version before deployment using simulated data under the null hypothesis, with scenarios that can be randomized and expanded over time. We prove that, regardless of how updates are chosen or how many are proposed, the lifetime probability of ever deploying a version whose Type I error rate exceeds the allowed level remains bounded. This guarantees that every subsequent decision controls the Type I error rate at the target level across these scenarios. At the same time, updates with sufficiently low Type I error rates pass validation with high probability, allowing the analyst to continuously improve its performance without sacrificing rigor. In two examples involving evolving AI analysts for bioequivalence studies and product A/B tests, Type I error rates reached 0.098 and 0.183 without continual validation, compared with at most 0.045 and 0.044 with it, while retaining 82% and 96% of the power from optimally selected valid updates.

title: xVGAE: A Hierarchical Variational Graph Autoencoder for Exchangeable Graphs
summary: Graphs play a crucial role in many applications, ranging from drug discovery to social network modeling and astronomy. Generative models for graphs have substantially advanced in recent years, but we identify relatively simple scenarios where state-of-the-art models struggle to converge within a standard compute budget, or exhibit prohibitively slow generation times. We propose a generative architecture that achieves quality competitive with state-of-the-art models and is orders of magnitude faster at generation. Our approach is inspired by the Aldous-Hoover theorem, a classic representation theorem that characterizes any probability distribution of graphs that is invariant to permutations of node indices or exchangeable. This theorem establishes that three ingredients suffice: a graph-level latent variable, a set of exchangeable node-specific latent variables, and a so-called graphon function that maps graph- and node-level variables to the probability of an edge between any node pair. Given a training set of graphs, our exchangeable Variational Graph AutoEncoder (xVGAE) learns an approximation to their underlying graphons, as well as graph- and node-level latent variables. We show that our xVGAE encodes latent representations that correlate with graph- and node-level properties, and can (quickly, in one shot) generate new graphs that closely match key training set statistics.

title: Robust Power and Sample Size Calculations in Quasi-likelihood Models: Methods and Practice
summary: Accurate power and sample size (PSS) calculations are essential for designing studies that use quasi-likelihood (QL) models, which extend generalized linear models (GLMs) to settings where the full distribution of the outcome is not specified. Traditional PSS approaches often rely on restrictive distributional assumptions, limiting their applicability when responses have non-standard distributions, variance functions are misspecified, or when predictors exhibit complex dependence structures. Building on recent advances in effect size measures for PSS - specifically, 2 Standard Deviations in the Linear Predictor (2SLiP) and Pseudo-Partial $R^2$ (P2R2) - developed with interpretability in mind, this paper extends and evaluates these effect size measures in the QL framework, keying in particular on their utility in PSS. We assess their empirical performance for the Wald test and then extend to the score test through extensive simulations across diverse outcome types, link functions, and variance structures. To illustrate practical utility, we applied these effect size measures to survey data on frontline health care workers from \citet{cahill2022occupational} to quantify the association between perceived personal protective equipment adequacy and mental health outcomes during the COVID-19 pandemic, adjusting for covariates. Our findings demonstrate that both 2SLiP and P2R2 provide robust and interpretable alternatives to traditional methods, maintaining accuracy with minimal distributional assumptions and enhancing the flexibility of PSS for realistic study designs.

title: Robust M-Estimation for Spliced Power-Law Models Under Cusp-Type Non-Regularity
summary: Statistical modeling of heavy-tailed data with bounded or finite body behaviour often relies on composite or spliced distributions characterized by structural thresholds. Because the probability density function features a sharp directional shift (a cusp) at the join point, the classical log-likelihood function exhibits a discontinuity in its first derivative, causing standard Cramér-Rao regularity conditions and maximum likelihood frameworks to break down. To overcome this non-regularity, we develop a robust, log-transformed asymmetric Huber M-estimation framework for the structural threshold, coupled with conditional shape maximum likelihood estimators. We derive a closed-form parameter-balancing condition that analytically guarantees Fisher consistency under structural tail asymmetry. Furthermore, we establish the joint asymptotic normality of the hybrid Maximum Likelihood and M-estimator system and derive its explicit sandwich covariance structure. A computationally efficient profiled Z-estimation algorithm is implemented to reduce the joint estimation to a one-dimensional root-finding problem. Finite-sample properties are validated through Monte Carlo simulations, and the practical utility of the framework is demonstrated on the benchmark Danish Fire Insurance claims dataset.

title: Robust Power and Sample Size Calculations in Quasi-likelihood Models: Methods and Practice
summary: Accurate power and sample size (PSS) calculations are essential for designing studies that use quasi-likelihood (QL) models, which extend generalized linear models (GLMs) to settings where the full distribution of the outcome is not specified. Traditional PSS approaches often rely on restrictive distributional assumptions, limiting their applicability when responses have non-standard distributions, variance functions are misspecified, or when predictors exhibit complex dependence structures. We assess their empirical performance for the Wald test and then extend to the score test through extensive simulations across diverse outcome types, link functions, and variance structures. To illustrate practical utility, we applied these effect size measures to survey data on frontline health care workers from \citet{cahill2022occupational} to quantify the association between perceived personal protective equipment adequacy and mental health outcomes during the COVID-19 pandemic, adjusting for covariates. Our findings demonstrate that both 2SLiP and P2R2 provide robust and interpretable alternatives to traditional methods, maintaining accuracy with minimal distributional assumptions and enhancing the flexibility of PSS for realistic study designs.

title: Continuous-depth Deep Gaussian Processes
summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are appealing Bayesian regression models, but their standard discrete-depth parameterization often becomes harder to optimize as depth grows. We argue that depth is better treated as a latent continuous evolution than as a long discrete stack. We therefore propose a continuous-depth formulation in which the latent representation follows a stochastic differential equation with a depth-indexed drift family equipped with a GP-based prior. This reframes the core design choice as the prior placed on that family, rather than adopting a purely neural continuous-depth parameterization as in neural ODE or neural SDE models. We study two instantiations of this idea: CDGP, a direct GP prior over the state--depth drift, and FlowDGP, a flow-evolved prior that captures richer depth dependence at lower training cost. To motivate the redesign, we analyze how the single-sample DGP objective can become increasingly sensitive under repeated layer composition, while residual DGP is a useful first repair that still remains a finite discrete construction. We also give pathwise sensitivity analysis for the continuous-depth formulation. Experiments on synthetic, benchmark, and large-scale regression tasks show that residual DGP improves over plain DGP, while CDGP and FlowDGP provide a stronger overall story across the regimes we study.

title: Dimension-free regimes for unadjusted Langevin in ridge-separable models: A subspace robust Wasserstein analysis
summary: The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) is widely used for high-dimensional Bayesian inference. Classical analyses in Wasserstein-2 distance predict an asymptotic bias and a mixing time that grow with dimension, but this metric is stronger than necessary for many statistical tasks. We instead analyze the bias in subspace robust Wasserstein distance, which controls the mean and arbitrary low-dimensional marginals and is therefore well suited to observables typically estimated in practice. For ridge-separable potentials formed with i.i.d. data, we prove high-probability bounds showing a bell-shaped mixing profile as the number of data points $N$ varies relative to the dimension $d$. In the overparameterized regime, the effective dimension is the rank $N$ of the data-dependent perturbation, leading to complexity depending on $N$ rather than $d$. In the large-sample regime, Gaussian-perturbation estimates yield dimension-free complexity once $N$ is sufficiently large. In contrast, near the proportional regime $\asymp d$, we prove that dimension-free guarantees are impossible in general.

title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via Generalized Moment Matching
summary: We study $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differentially private synthetic data for arbitrary databases of $n$ records in $[-1,1]^d$ under a specified integral probability metric (IPM). We introduce generalized moment matching, which estimates moments privately, fits a probability measure, and samples synthetic records. A general error theorem applies when moment error controls the target IPM. This framework extends Chebyshev moment matching for $1$-Wasserstein distance and smooth queries. We apply the framework to maximum mean discrepancy with Matern and Laplace kernels and a two-layer ReLU neural tangent kernel.We also obtain guarantees for sliced Wasserstein-$1$ and the IPM induced by norm-bounded ReLU networks. With sufficiently many synthetic records,these rates are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed dimension.

title: Behavioral Mapping of Hierarchical Dynamical Models Accelerates Bayesian Parameter Inference
summary: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is often limited by the cost of repeated model simulation. We present a behavioral mapping framework that uses the inferred posterior of a higher-level model to accelerate inference of a lower-level model without requiring state or parameter correspondence between them. Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, we define the notion of behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. We learn a level set of behavioral support using a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed model parameter proposals before expensive simulations during Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference. We derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set retains all detailed model parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance. We apply this method to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data. After initial setup costs, our approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.

title: Random Projections for Spectral Algorithms: Optimal Rates in Sobolev Norms
summary: Random projections (RP) offer an effective method for reducing computational and storage overhead while preserving the geometric structure of data. However, existing studies have primarily focused on the optimal generalization performance of specific kernel-regularized algorithms with RP in the well-specified setting and under restrictive conditions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of the generalization performance of RP-based spectral algorithms under general conditions \change{without sacrificing statistical efficiency}. By leveraging the embedding property of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and a refined analysis of the operator similarity, we establish optimal learning rates in Sobolev norms that match the minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. For two common implementations of RP, randomized sketches and Nyström sub-sampling (uniform or leverage-based), we show that the projection dimension required for optimality is proportional to the average or maximal effective dimension, yielding a significant reduction in computational cost while maintaining the statistical efficiency. Our results do not rely on the uniform boundedness assumption on the regression function and are valid across a wide range of source conditions, i.e., $s> α_0-1/β$, where $s,β$, and $α_0$ denote the smoothness index, capacity index, and the embedding index, respectively. In the benign case when $α_0=1/β$, the optimality holds for all $s\in (0,2τ]$ with $τ$ and $γ$ denoting the qualification index and norm index. Experimental results demonstrate both the theoretical validity and the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Bridge change-of-measure for propagator estimation of diffusions
summary: The propagator of one-dimensional diffusions has relevant applications in statistical inference and across many disciplines. Yet it is obtained in closed form only for very few simple models. Here we analyze an importance sampling strategy based on a bridge change of measure to estimate propagators: paths are generated under an auxiliary diffusion whose bridge between the two fixed boundary points is easy to generate, and the target propagator is recovered through a Radon-Nikodym derivative or likelihood ratio correction derived from Girsanov's theorem. This method overcomes the main limitations of the crude Monte Carlo estimator, which relies on binning in state space, introducing bias and becoming inefficient with rare transitions. We apply the method to a range of benchmark processes and show that the bridge-based estimator matches the accuracy of crude Monte Carlo with orders of magnitude fewer sample paths. Finally, we elaborate on discretization schemes for the Radon-Nikodym derivative and on approximations to the best-in-class change of measure, both of which increase the efficiency of the method.

title: Estimating Group Average Treatment Effects in High-Risk Populations with Unobserved Target Membership
summary: Estimating treatment effects within a prespecified high-risk population is challenging. When risk status is unobserved or the target population is small, analyses restricted to high-risk individuals can be unstable or inefficient. We propose a risk-score-weighted soft-targeting (RSW) estimator for group average treatment effects in high-risk populations. It accommodates two settings: when high-risk status is observed, the membership probability can be estimated within the analysis sample; when unobserved, it can be obtained from a reference model using covariates in the analysis sample. RSW uses these probabilities to represent the target population, learns a doubly robust treatment effect in the full sample, and aggregates a low-dimensional treatment-effect surface over the risk-weighted target distribution. We establish pointwise asymptotic normality and an influence-function-based variance estimator. In simulations with continuous and binary outcomes, RSW had similar bias and lower variance than two hard-targeting alternatives. Sensitivity analyses showed that the gain persisted when treatment-effect sufficiency was violated, although RSW bias increased under strong violations. We applied the method to the All of Us study to estimate effects of non-GLP antidiabetic and antihypertensive medication use on mild cognitive impairment (MCI)-free time restricted at 48 months within comorbidity-defined high-risk subgroups. We estimated the risk score in a nonoverlapping internal reference sample and applied it to the outcome-analysis sample. This illustrates how soft targeting can improve precision while retaining an interpretable high-risk target population.

title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
summary: Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.

title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
summary: Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.

title: Beyond Global Importance: A Heterogeneity Index for Sensitivity Analysis
summary: Global sensitivity analysis quantifies how strongly inputs influence a model output, however, input importance often varies across the model space. We introduce a heterogeneity index H to quantify this variation. The index compares normalized regional sensitivity profiles using mean pairwise total-variation distance and its values range from zero to one. We test H on nine benchmark functions and examine its robustness to the number of regions, sample size, and sampling strategy. We further demonstrate it using models of wooden-pallet carbon footprint, flood risk, and steel-structure reliability. Across these cases, H reveals changes in sensitivity that global indices obscure, including inputs whose importance changes substantially across the model space and differences between rare behavioral regimes. The index complements global sensitivity analysis by indicating when a single global sensitivity profile is insufficient. An open-source implementation is provided in the simdec package.

title: Bayes Factor Testing of Linear and Nonlinear Effects in Additive Gaussian Process Regression
summary: Gaussian process regression flexibly models nonlinear relationships between predictors and an outcome variable. A central question in this modeling framework is whether each predictor affects the outcome linearly, nonlinearly, or not at all. We propose a Bayesian testing framework for this problem within additive Gaussian process regression. Each predictor is decomposed into a standardized linear component with a $g$-prior and an orthogonalized Gaussian process component capturing nonlinear structure. The latter is governed by a standardized magnitude parameter whose value zero removes the component. Local and non-local priors are considered for the standardized magnitude parameter. Bayes factors for testing the linear and nonlinear effects are computed from the fitted full model via Savage-Dickey-type identities, avoiding expensive marginal likelihood computations of many different models. To assess the accuracy of the Bayes factor estimates, the outcomes are compared to bridge sampling estimates. Simulations and empirical applications show the performance and applicability of the methodology.

title: Metric Conformal Prediction via the Conditional Expected Local Radius
summary: We introduce the conditional expected local radius (CELR) and develop a new conformal prediction method for non-Euclidean responses in general metric spaces. CELR measures local conditional probability concentration, allowing prediction sets to accommodate heterogeneity and multimodality without requiring densities or a vector space structure. Its conditional distribution yields a nonconformity score that is comparable across covariate values and avoids costly transport comparisons between distance profiles. We further adapt a metric distributional random forest that handles multivariate covariates and nonlinear interactions, while a single forest fit supplies all score components, reducing computation by eliminating repeated local fitting. We establish uniform consistency of the estimators and asymptotic conditional validity under suitable regularity conditions, together with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability. Numerical studies demonstrate effective uncertainty quantification across different metric spaces and substantial computational savings over the conditional profile score method.

title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Likelihood Ratio Tests for the Power Spherical Distribution
summary: The Power Spherical distribution has been proposed as a computationally efficient alternative to the von Mises-Fisher distribution for data on the unit sphere, with reduced computational cost for simulation and a simpler normalizing constant. Despite these advantages, its statistical inference properties remain underdeveloped. In this paper, we develop a likelihood-based framework for estimation and inference for the Power Spherical distribution. Within this framework, we develop maximum likelihood estimation procedures for both the central direction and concentration parameter. Building on these estimators, we formulate likelihood ratio tests for hypotheses involving known and unknown parameters, study their asymptotic behavior, and evaluate finite-sample performance through simulation studies. The results demonstrate accurate Type I error control and good power when the asymptotic chi-square approximation is appropriate, while the parametric bootstrap provides reliable inference in small-sample settings or those where the dimension is large relative to the sample size. The findings also highlight nontrivial dependence of the power of tests for the central direction on the concentration parameter.

title: On the Calibration of Isotonic Distributional Regression
comment: Accepted at AISTATS 2026 - Workshop on Calibration for Modern AI
summary: Isotonic distributional regression (IDR) has recently been proposed as a non-parametric technique for probabilistic forecasting via the estimation of conditional distributions under order restrictions, based on continuous outcomes from deterministic model outputs. IDR has been widely used and multiple studies report promising performance and well-calibrated forecasts across application domains. We document a peculiar out-of-sample artifact of IDR, where probability integral transform (PIT) values are rational fractions with empirical frequencies resembling Thomae's function, an effect which thus far seems to have been overlooked. This phenomenon is demonstrated empirically using meteorological data and a simulation study. We further provide a theoretical explanation linking the spiking behavior to the discrete structure of the isotonic fits, and discuss how this artifact can be mitigated via smoothing approaches.

title: Generalized Infinite Hidden Markov Models
summary: We introduce a flexible Bayesian nonparametric hidden Markov model for longitudinal data based on the hidden hierarchical Dirichlet process. Unlike the classical infinite hidden Markov model, the proposed model allows transition probabilities to change over time. In particular, this model provides a framework that operates between homogeneous and heterogeneous Markov model formulations, allowing the rows of the transition probability matrix to be clustered ac- cording to their temporal evolution. Inference is performed through a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, which enables the joint estimation of model parameters, latent variables, and number of states, within a unified framework. Simulation studies under both homogeneous and heterogeneous transition regimes show that the proposed model tends to recover the true latent structure, whereas the infinite hidden Markov model tends to overestimate the number of states when transitions vary over time. Two applications illustrate the ability of the model to detect changes in the transition dynamics.

title: Nonparametric autoregressive estimation of probability distributions with parallel gradient boosting
summary: Nonparametric estimation of joint probability distributions is a core problem in statistics, which is notoriously challenging with high-dimensional data. Such challenges also arise with conditional distribution estimation and have led to flexible algorithms that aim to tackle the ''curse of dimensionality'' by exploiting predictive structures of lower dimension than the ambient space. In this paper, we study the use of such conditional distribution estimators to estimate joint distributions by factorizing the latter in an ''autoregressive'' way. We show that for loss functions satisfying a subadditivity property, bounds on the convergence rate of an autoregressive estimator can be derived from bounds on the convergence rate of the conditional distribution estimators. These bounds relate the difficulty of estimating the joint distribution to that of estimating the most challenging factor in the autoregressive factorization. When the conditional estimators adapt to sparsity in their conditioning sets, we characterize this difficulty through variable elimination in an undirected dependence graph. This allows bounding the rates of convergence by quantities related to the sparsity of the graph, and provides an additional motivation for the autoregressive approach. We then evaluate the practical performance of an autoregressive estimator based on parallel gradient boosting, a flexible nonparametric method for estimating conditional distributions. The estimator demonstrates competitive estimation performance on various simulated and real datasets, even without optimizing the factorization order. Together, these results support nonparametric autoregressive estimation as a practical approach to flexible joint distribution estimation.

title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
summary: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

title: More efficient transportation of causal effects using mediators
summary: We develop flexible semiparametric estimators of the average treatment effect transported to a target population that leverage mediators to achieve identification, and prior knowledge of population heterogeneity or summary-level statistics to achieve improved efficiency. We first propose a one-step semiparametric estimator that assumes knowledge of the baseline covariates driving the heterogeneity across populations. This approach improves efficiency by transporting only through these covariates, rather than through the full covariate set. We then introduce a collaborative one-step semiparametric estimator that also improves efficiency without requiring knowledge of which covariates drive study heterogeneity. Collectively, these estimators advance our ability to transport causal effects by improving efficiency in the presence of mediation and intermediate confounding through targeted dimension reduction strategies. We use simulation to examine finite-sample performance and apply our estimators to a large-scale housing mobility trial (MTO) and a hearing intervention trial (ACHIEVE).

title: Lifetime-valid decisions by continually evolving AI analysts
summary: AI agents increasingly act as analysts whose decision can often be cast as hypothesis tests. Classical tests control the Type I error rate, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, for fixed procedures. However, AI analysts introduce internal randomness and can evolve continuously over time. As AI analysts evolve, the risk of approving versions with Type I error rates above the target can accumulate, and adaptive use of evaluation feedback can lead to overfitting. We introduce continual validation, which evaluates each proposed AI analyst version before deployment using simulated data under the null hypothesis, with scenarios that can be randomized and expanded over time. We prove that, regardless of how updates are chosen or how many are proposed, the lifetime probability of ever deploying a version whose Type I error rate exceeds the allowed level remains bounded. This guarantees that every subsequent decision controls the Type I error rate at the target level across these scenarios. At the same time, updates with sufficiently low Type I error rates pass validation with high probability, allowing the analyst to continuously improve its performance without sacrificing rigor. In two examples involving evolving AI analysts for bioequivalence studies and product A/B tests, Type I error rates reached 0.098 and 0.183 without continual validation, compared with at most 0.045 and 0.044 with it, while retaining 82% and 96% of the power from optimally selected valid updates.

title: A Subjective Bayesian Approach to Address Unchecked Assumptions in a Causal Analysis
summary: Causal analyses using observational data rely on identifying assumptions that cannot be verified from the observed data alone. When such unchecked assumptions fail, effect estimates may be biased and uncertainty may be understated. We propose the Adjusted Model for Unchecked Assumptions (AMUA), a subjective Bayesian framework that propagates uncertainty about the joint validity of key causal assumptions through a two-component posterior mixture. One component corresponds to the standard observational causal model in which the assumptions hold (referred to as the "assumption-hold component"); the other represents a flexibly defined model that allows the causal assumptions to fail (referred to as the "assumption-fail component"). The mixture weight $π$ is specified by the analyst as the prior probability assigned to the assumption-hold component. This formulation leads to a new diagnostic, $π_{\min}$: the smallest value of $π$ for which the 95\% HPD set for the average treatment effect (ATE) excludes zero. In simulations with a spatially structured unmeasured confounder, we evaluate bias, interval length, and coverage as $π$ varies. The results show that acknowledging assumption uncertainty can widen intervals, and improve coverage relative to analyses that treat the assumptions as certain. In a county-level application relating long-term PM$_{2.5}$ exposure to COVID-19 mortality, AMUA shows how posterior conclusions depend on prior confidence in the identifying assumptions.

title: Volatility-Corrected Prediction Intervals: Locally Adaptive Uncertainty Quantification for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Prediction intervals from probabilistic time-series forecasters are commonly assessed by marginal coverage, the long-run proportion of observations falling inside the intervals. However, forecast errors in time series are often serially dependent and heteroskedastic, so prediction intervals can attain near-nominal marginal coverage while miscovering systematically during periods of larger local error variance. We identify and address this failure mode, which we call \emph{local scale miscalibration}. We first document the phenomenon using time-series foundation models (TSFMs): across several real-world series, their native intervals often attain near-nominal marginal coverage while exhibiting substantial temporal variation in local coverage, alternating between overcoverage and undercoverage over shorter windows. We then propose Volatility-Corrected Prediction Intervals (VCPI), a post-hoc calibration procedure that uses the base forecaster's predictive scale as a baseline, models the volatility of standardized forecast residuals with a Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) model, and applies a multiplicative correction to produce locally adaptive prediction intervals. We justify VCPI both theoretically and empirically, comparing it against model-agnostic conformal counterparts. We provide a theoretical analysis of interval adaptation of the proposed method following abrupt changes in volatility. Empirically, we evaluate VCPI on Chronos, Moirai, and TimesFM across four real-world datasets and find that it produces more stable local coverage than conformal baselines while maintaining near-nominal marginal coverage and comparable interval width.

title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
summary: Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.

title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
summary: Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.

title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
summary: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.
